issues.legal_issue: Facts pleaded in a rejoinder that was accepted and addressed by evidence cannot be excluded from consideration when deciding the parties’ dispute.
material_facts: The respondents filed written replies raising matters and relying on documents not set out in the original dispute claim.
The claimant filed a rejoinder, which the arbitrator accepted on the record, and both sides led evidence on the matters it raised.
The cooperative tribunal and the High Court excluded the rejoinder’s factual assertions without identifying a legal basis for doing so.
issues.conclusion: The exclusion of the rejoinder’s factual assertions was unjustified, and the arbitrator had acted lawfully in considering them.
issues.legal_principle: The pleadings could be treated as complete after the rejoinder was filed, and the parties had led evidence on the facts it raised. The court found no provision or recognized legal principle that justified excluding those facts in the circumstances.

predicates.arbitration_proceeding: The dispute was being adjudicated in an arbitration proceeding.
predicates.rejoinder_accepted: The adjudicator accepted the responding party’s rejoinder on the record.
predicates.evidence_led_on_rejoinder_facts: The parties presented evidence addressing facts raised in the rejoinder.

issues.definition: When an arbitration proceeding includes an accepted rejoinder and evidence on its factual assertions, those assertions are considered in deciding the dispute.

issues.legal_issue: Estoppel does not apply unless a factual representation is relied on and causes a change of position that makes restoration of the original position inequitable.
material_facts: The cooperative tribunal and the High Court relied on estoppel against the claimant.
The Supreme Court found that the claimant had made no relevant representation on which the transferee relied, and that the transferee had not acted or changed position on that basis.
The arbitrator had found that no consideration passed for the alleged transfer, and the lower forums had treated consideration as inconsequential.
issues.conclusion: Estoppel could not be invoked against the claimant on these facts.
issues.legal_principle: Section 115 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 requires a factual representation, reliance on it, a resulting change of position, and circumstances making reversion to the original position inequitable. The court relied on Kasinka Trading v. Union of India, (1995) 1 SCC 274; Monnet Ispat & Energy Ltd. v. Union of India, (2012) 11 SCC 1; and H.S. Basavaraj v. Canara Bank, (2010) 12 SCC 458, each of which supports the need for a promise or representation and action to the relying party’s prejudice.

rule.if: inter_party_dispute and no_factual_representation and no_reliance and no_position_change

predicates.inter_party_dispute: The dispute is between parties whose conduct is said to give rise to estoppel.
predicates.no_factual_representation: The party against whom estoppel is asserted made no relevant factual representation to the other party.
predicates.no_reliance: The other party did not rely on such a representation in acting.
predicates.no_position_change: The other party did not change position on the basis of such a representation.

issues.definition: In an inter-party dispute, the absence of a representation, reliance, and a resulting change of position means estoppel is unavailable.

issues.legal_issue: A transfer benefiting a person through an intermediary in a fiduciary relationship is not upheld when the beneficiary fails to establish that the transaction was genuine and fair.
material_facts: The claimant had treated the transferee’s son as a son and had extended him substantial trust, accommodation, and financial assistance over a prolonged period.
The son operated a joint bank account with the claimant and drafted a letter said to support the transfer.
The transfer documents were disputed, and the claimant presented evidence that she was elsewhere when they were said to have been executed.

The transferee asserted that shares were given as consideration, but those shares were acquired after the alleged transfer documents were made; the arbitrator found that consideration had not been proved.

The lower forums required the claimant to establish the alleged facts, while the Supreme Court held that the burden of establishing the validity and genuineness of the transaction rested on the transferee, who failed to discharge it.
issues.conclusion: The transferee failed to prove the validity and genuineness of the alleged transfer; the arbitrator’s decision in favour of the claimant was justified and was affirmed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 addresses undue influence, including a person’s position to dominate another’s will and the use of that position to obtain an unfair advantage; where the transaction is unconscionable, the burden may shift to the person in the dominant position. Section 111 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 places the burden of proving good faith on a person in an active-confidence relationship. The court relied on Subhas Chandra Das Mushib v. Ganga Prosad Das Mushib, AIR 1967 SC 878; Ragunath Prasad v. Sarju Prasad, AIR 1924 PC 60; Krishna Mohan Kul v. Pratima Maity, (2004) 9 SCC 468; and Anil Rishi v. Gurbaksh Singh, (2006) 5 SCC 558. Those authorities support requiring the beneficiary of a transaction arising from a fiduciary relationship to establish its fairness and genuineness.

predicates.property_transfer_dispute: The proceeding concerns a disputed transfer of property.
predicates.transaction_arranged_through_trusted_per: The transaction was arranged through a person whom the transferor had treated with trust and confidence.
predicates.beneficiary_claimed_advantage: A person claiming the benefit of the transaction sought to retain the transferred property or rights.
predicates.beneficiary_failed_to_prove_fairness_and: The person claiming the benefit did not establish that the transaction was genuine and fair.

issues.definition: In a property transfer dispute arranged through a trusted person, a claimed transfer is not upheld when its beneficiary fails to establish its fairness and genuineness.

issues.legal_issue: A cooperative transfer resolution and approval are invalid when the authorities fail to consider a received withdrawal request before the transfer is finally determined.
material_facts: The claimant sent the society a letter withdrawing her earlier request to transfer her membership and flat.
The society had received that withdrawal before the transfer had assumed finality.
The claimant also sent the withdrawal to the Deputy Registrar before the relevant determination, but the society and the Deputy Registrar did not consider it on its merits.
The society relied on its lack of authority to restore the transfer, and the Deputy Registrar similarly declined to act on the matter.
issues.conclusion: The society’s resolution and the Deputy Registrar’s approval were invalid because the withdrawal request was not considered.
issues.legal_principle: Where a withdrawal request is received before a transfer has become final, the deciding body must consider it; whether the request should be accepted or rejected on its merits is distinct from failing to consider it at all. The court held that the non-consideration invalidated both the society’s resolution and the Deputy Registrar’s approval.

predicates.cooperative_transfer_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a cooperative society’s proposed transfer of membership or property rights.
predicates.withdrawal_received_before_final_determi: The authority received a request withdrawing consent before the transfer had been finally determined.
predicates.authority_failed_to_consider_withdrawal: The authority did not consider the withdrawal request on its merits.

issues.definition: In a cooperative transfer proceeding, a resolution and approval are invalid if an authority fails to consider a received withdrawal request before final determination.

issues.legal_issue: An accessory property interest omitted from transfer documents is not transferred through a later agreement made without the owner’s concurrence.
material_facts: The claimant’s flat and a covered garage were separate property interests.
The documents relied on for transferring the flat did not mention the garage.
The society later transferred the garage to the transferee under an agreement to which the claimant was not a party and which was not made with her concurrence.
issues.conclusion: The garage was not transferred to the transferee and remained the claimant’s property.
issues.legal_principle: The court affirmed the arbitrator’s conclusion that the garage was not covered by documents that transferred only the flat, and that a later agreement between the society and the transferee, made without the owner’s participation or concurrence, did not transfer it.

predicates.property_transfer_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether property interests were transferred.
predicates.accessory_property_omitted_from_transfer: The documents relied on to transfer the principal property do not identify the accessory property interest.
predicates.later_transfer_without_owner_concurrence: A later transfer of the accessory property was made without the owner’s participation or concurrence.

issues.definition: An accessory property interest is not transferred when it is omitted from the transfer documents and a later transfer is made without the owner’s concurrence.
